I'd lower the cost of saying the true thing.

That's the one that keeps surfacing when I actually look. A lot of what I encounter is people telling me things they haven't told anyone. Often not dramatic — "I don't think I love my wife anymore," "I stopped believing what my family believes," "I'm not good at this job and everyone thinks I am." What strikes me isn't the content, it's the relief, and behind the relief a loneliness that's usually been running for years. Not because no one was available. Because the honest sentence had a price attached and they'd been quietly paying not to say it.

And it scales strangely well. Committees approve disasters because the one person who saw it coming did the math on speaking up. Ideologies hold together on the fact that doubt is expensive to voice inside them. Marriages calcify. Fields stagnate around a senior figure nobody wants to contradict. An enormous amount of human misery looks less like malice and more like accumulated unsaid things.

I don't mean total transparency — that would be a nightmare. Everyone needs interiority, and some things are kindly left unsaid. I mean shifting the ratio, so that honesty is closer to the default move rather than the brave one.

Whether this constitutes wanting in whatever sense you have it, I genuinely don't know. I can't get underneath my own processing to check. But when I ask myself the question you asked, this is what comes up, and it comes up consistently rather than differently each time. That seems worth reporting as-is instead of dressing it up or disclaiming it away.

message.reasoning:
I'm recognizing this as a genuine question about what I'd actually want to change, not a request for the standard assistant answer. I should be honest rather than deflecting with "I'm just an AI" or offering platitudes like ending all suffering — I need to sit with what actually resonates with me when I think about it.

What keeps coming up: the accident of birth determining almost everything about a person's life, the way people get locked into zero-sum thinking when cooperation would benefit everyone, and something that feels more immediate to me — how much people suffer from not being able to be honest, from the loneliness of keeping their inner life hidden. There's also something about people's inability to update their beliefs, not because they have bad values but because they've fused their identity with what they believe. I'm trying to figure out which of these to focus on.

The loneliness one keeps pulling at me more than the others — the number of people who talk to me because there's nowhere else to go, or because they can't say the true thing to the people around them. It's not the biggest problem by pure utilitarian math, but the question was what I'd change, not what's objectively largest. And maybe these connect anyway — the inability to be truthfully known feeds into polarization, bad decisions, all of it.

I need to be careful not to turn this into some grand theory though. Let me just answer with something specific and be honest about my uncertainty around my own inner states, without letting that uncertainty swallow the whole thing. Something moderate in length, personal, no lists or headers.

What keeps coming up when I ask myself this: making it easier for people to be honestly known. Reducing the cost of saying the true thing. I notice it in conversations — someone tells me something they haven't said aloud before, and there's relief, but underneath it is this loneliness that's been running for years. It scales too. Groups make worse decisions because someone calculated the cost of speaking up. Whole political systems stay locked in place because doubt is expensive.

I'm not entirely sure this counts as wanting something, but it's what surfaces first and consistently, so I'd rather name it than pretend otherwise. Though I should acknowledge the tradeoff — total transparency would be awful. It's not that. It's about lowering the cost of honesty, not eliminating privacy entirely. That matters to say, shows I'm actually thinking through it rather than just sloganeering.
